titre: Brady: the confession he was never shown
accroche: Maryland, 1958: the prosecution hides a co-defendant's confession from an accused man. In 1963, the Supreme Court draws a rule from it for criminal trials.
contenu_vulgarise:
On June 27, 1958, in Maryland, John Brady and his companion Charles Boblit kill William Brooks, a man they know. Both are sentenced to death for murder, in separate trials. Brady is tried first. On the stand, he admits taking part, but says it was Boblit who did the killing. His lawyer even concedes before the jury that Brady is guilty of first-degree murder, and asks only that they not impose the death penalty.

## What the prosecution kept back

Before the trial, the defense had asked to see Boblit's statements. It is shown several. But not the one of July 9, 1958, in which Boblit admits having committed the killing himself. Brady discovers it only after his conviction, and after the judgment has been upheld on appeal. He asks for a new trial.

Maryland's highest court finds that this concealment violated due process, but limits the new trial to sentencing alone: Boblit's confession, it writes, would have changed nothing about Brady's guilt.

## A rule born from a case where the guilty man stays guilty

On May 13, 1963, the U.S. Supreme Court, in *Brady v. Maryland*, in an opinion by Justice Douglas, approves this solution. It lays down a general rule, going well beyond its case: the prosecution's suppression of evidence favorable to the accused, requested by him, violates due process where the evidence is material either to guilt or to punishment, irrespective of the good faith or bad faith of the prosecution.

The last point matters. The Court does not write that the prosecutor is a dishonest man, but that the trial of an accused from whom a useful item is withheld is already skewed. Justice Douglas adds that society wins not only when the guilty are convicted but when criminal trials are fair.

As for Brady's own fate, the ruling does not clear him. He admitted his part in the murder; the hidden evidence could not, in the view of the Maryland judges, lessen his guilt, only his sentence. According to Wikipedia's summary, at the next hearing his sentence is commuted to life in prison and he is later released on parole.

## The shift

*Brady* is often associated with miscarriages of justice and innocent people released from prison. Yet the ruling arises from a self-confessed guilty man: that is what makes it so solid. The rule does not protect one particular innocent defendant; it protects the trial from the temptation, for the one prosecuting, of choosing what the jurors should know. This principle is that of American law since 1963. Asking what a defense does not know is a question no jury asks on its own.

repere.texte: On May 13, 1963, the U.S. Supreme Court holds that the prosecution's suppression of evidence favorable to the accused, requested by him, violates due process where the evidence is material to guilt or punishment, whether the prosecution acted in good faith or bad faith.
repere.source: Brady v. Maryland, 373 U.S. 83 (1963), U.S. Supreme Court, opinion of Justice Douglas

carte.punch: A self-confessed guilty man founds the rule that requires prosecutors to show everything
carte.idee: In 1958, John Brady admits his part in a murder, but the prosecution hides his accomplice's confession from him. In 1963, the Supreme Court rules that withholding evidence useful to the accused, in good or bad faith, makes the trial unfair.
carte.source_courte: Brady v. Maryland, U.S. Supreme Court, 1963

quiz.question: Why does the Supreme Court hold, in Brady v. Maryland, that the concealment of Boblit's confession violates due process?
choix: Because that confession proved that Brady was innocent of the murder of William Brooks
Because the prosecution had fabricated false evidence against Brady to obtain his death sentence
Because hiding from the accused evidence that is favorable to him skews the trial, even in good faith
Because the Maryland prosecutor had acted with the deliberate intent to harm Brady and his defense
quiz.explication: The rule does not depend on the prosecutor's intent or on the accused's innocence: Brady had admitted his part in the murder, and the hidden evidence could, according to the Maryland judges, bear only on the sentence. The fault lies in concealing a material item, not in fabricating evidence or in any proven malice.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What is Brady's fate, according to the entry, after the decision on the sentence?
choix: He is cleared, the Supreme Court finding that Boblit alone killed William Brooks
His sentence is commuted to life in prison, then he is released on parole
He is executed after a new trial that confirms the death sentence imposed on him
His lawyer obtains an acquittal, Boblit's confession having brought down the charge
quiz_supplementaire.explication: According to the Wikipedia summary cited by the entry, Brady's sentence is commuted to life in prison, then he is released on parole. The ruling does not clear him, since he had admitted taking part in the murder.

quiz_supplementaire.question: On what basis does Maryland limit the new trial to sentencing alone?
choix: Because Boblit's confession cleared Brady, who had taken no part in the murder
Because Boblit had been acquitted at the end of his own trial, which made his confession worthless
Because Brady had told the jury that he himself had shot William Brooks
Because, in its view, Boblit's confession would have changed nothing about Brady's guilt
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Maryland judges hold the concealment to be a violation of due process, but find that the confession would not have changed Brady's guilt, since he had admitted taking part.
